review.assessment: This change introduces `retryd/budget.py`, which defines constants for a 1-hour window and a limit of 3 retries per window, alongside a `Budget` class intended to track spent allowances. However, the implementation contains a critical bug in `window_key` that ignores the provided event timestamp entirely. As a result, every call maps to a single static window key derived only from process start time, breaking the intended per-hour budgeting logic and causing retries to permanently halt after three total events instead of resetting hourly.

findings.actual: Identical keys (`0`), because the method ignores `ts` and only computes `self.started_at // WINDOW_SECONDS`.
findings.call: python -c "from retryd.budget import Budget; b = Budget(1000); print(b.window_key(1), b.window_key(3700))"
findings.defect: `window_key` completely ignores its `ts` argument, mapping every event to the same static window key regardless of when it occurred.
findings.expected: Different window keys corresponding to the two distinct timestamps (e.g., accounting for a 3600s gap).

findings.actual: `False`, because a single permanent counter is incremented forever, permanently blocking further retries regardless of elapsed time.
findings.call: python -c "from retryd.budget import Budget; b = Budget(1000); [b.spend(i) for i in range(3)]; print(b.has_room(999))"
findings.defect: Because `window_key` ignores timestamps, the budget never resets per hour. It acts as a flat lifetime counter, causing the SLA check to fail permanently after three retries.
findings.expected: `True`, as the budget should allow new attempts once an hour has passed since previous events.
